topics.title: Turnmark: short-round Up/Down prediction markets on CKB, live on testnet

recent_posts.topic_title: Turnmark: short-round Up/Down prediction markets on CKB, live on testnet
recent_posts.author: Adokiye_Destiny
recent_posts.content_text:
Turnmark lets you take a position on a simple question: will an asset’s price finish higher or lower over a fixed round?
We have BTC/USDT rounds running on Nervos testnet at two durations: 5 minutes and 15 minutes. You deposit test CKB into UP or DOWN before participation closes. The round compares committee-signed prices at its exact start and end boundaries. Winning shares can then be redeemed from the pool.
There is no order book and no house quoting odds. Participants on the two sides fund a shared pot. Your potential payout depends on how much is deposited on each side.
This is a working testnet application, not a mainnet launch. We are sharing it for people to try, review and help shape.
Try it: turnmark.astromind.cc — served over HTTPS.
Source: GitHub repository calledAdo/turnmark.
Addresses and repository paths are written as code here to avoid automatic links.
1. What a round looks like
Suppose a BTC/USDT round runs from 12:00 to 12:05:
Before participation closes, choose UP or DOWN and deposit test CKB. You receive shares tied to that specific pool and side.
Participation is sealed before 12:00. This gives the seal transaction time to confirm before the starting price becomes known.
The exact signed 12:00 SPOT update supplies the starting price, provided the pool also has valid evidence that participation was frozen beforehand.
The exact signed 12:05 SPOT update supplies the ending price.
A higher ending price makes UP the winner. A lower price makes DOWN the winner. An exact tie makes stakes refundable.
The five-minute duration describes the price interval. It does not mean deposits stay open until 12:00, or that payouts are ready exactly at 12:05. Oracle availability, transaction submission and CKB confirmation are separate steps.
You can withdraw while the pool remains OPEN. Once it is sealed, participation is fixed.
How payouts work
This is a parimutuel market: winners recover their stake and share the losing side’s pot, after the configured fee on that losing pot.
For example, with 10 CKB on UP and 10 CKB on DOWN, a 2% fee, and an UP result:
The losing pot contributes 9.8 CKB after the 0.2 CKB fee.
UP holders share 19.8 CKB in proportion to their winning shares.
A participant holding 1 CKB of the 10 CKB UP stake receives 1.98 CKB, before their transaction costs.
The displayed payout is an estimate while deposits and withdrawals can still change the pot. It is not a fixed return. A losing position loses its stake.
2. What lives on CKB
The protocol uses CKB cells and four contracts:
Piece
Responsibility
pool_type
Validates pool state transitions, boundary-price evidence, accounting and settlement.
pool_admin_lock
Separates lifecycle authority from creation and teardown authority.
share_xudt
Represents pool-specific UP and DOWN shares and constrains minting and burning.
treasury_lock
Guards the treasury used by the xUDT-backed pool path.
The public application currently uses CKB-backed pools. An xUDT path exists in the code, but the funded public-testnet acceptance described below does not establish that path’s readiness.
The core pool lifecycle is:
OPEN
Deposits and withdrawals allowed
|
| SEAL participation before the start boundary
v
SEALED
Participation frozen
|
| ACTIVATE with exact start price + freeze proof
v
LOCKED
Round running
|
| RESOLVE with exact end price
v
FINALIZED
Winning shares redeemable
Cancellation paths:
OPEN -> VOID if empty or one-sided at seal, or on timeout
SEALED -> VOID on activation timeout
LOCKED -> VOID on resolution timeout
VOID: stakes refundable
Exact tie: refund outcome
An exact tie follows the refund outcome. After the claim grace period, an authorized maintenance transaction can consume the terminal PoolCell.
3. Why sealing and starting are separate
This is one of the most important parts of the design.
If deposits and the starting price were fixed in one transaction submitted at the boundary, that transaction might confirm after the price was already known. Participation could remain open too late.
Turnmark separates those events:
SEAL freezes participation ahead of the boundary.
ACTIVATE records the exact boundary price and verifies a signed checkpoint covering the actual sealed cell’s origin.
The checkpoint binds the network, boundary and accepted chain history. The contract checks the sealed cell’s origin and its header ancestry against that certificate.
There is an explicit trust limit: the committee attests to its external observation time and accepted chain cut. CKB headers alone cannot prove that something happened before a real-world wall-clock deadline.
Without acceptable freeze evidence, the pool must not start. The timeout path allows cancellation and refunds instead.
4. Where the prices come from
Turnmark uses Lean Oracle, introduced in the Nervos Talk post “Asset price oracle on Nervos Network” (topic 10800, at talk.nervos.org/t/asset-price-oracle-on-nervos-network/10800). That post explains the oracle’s publishers, signed updates and public mirror; this post focuses on how Turnmark uses them for prediction rounds.
Turnmark consumes the oracle through lean-oracle-sdk. Oracle publishers, price production and the public mirror run independently of this project’s workers.
For settlement, the pool pins its feed, exponent and publisher committee. ACTIVATE and RESOLVE verify the signed update directly, including quorum signatures and the feed’s Merkle inclusion proof. The live publisher-set cell is referenced as a read-only cell dependency.
The current product uses boundary SPOT, not TWAP:
Start price: the signed update whose timestamp exactly equals the configured start boundary.
End price: the signed update whose timestamp exactly equals the configured close boundary.
A later price is not substituted simply because the required update is unavailable.
The browser’s live chart is informational. It is not settlement evidence. The contract verifies the signed boundary update supplied in the transaction.
This also means oracle methodology matters. An exact signed SPOT tick proves what the committee signed; it does not make instantaneous markets immune to manipulation or guarantee a price will always be available.
5. What the backend does—and what it cannot do
Workers keep rounds moving. They create pools, seal participation, obtain boundary proofs, submit activation and resolution transactions, handle timeout cancellations and eventually clean up terminal pools.
Each asset-duration pair is a separate lane. BTC/USDT 5m and BTC/USDT 15m have their own schedules and worker services.
Within each lane, wallet responsibilities are split:
Rail
Actions
Lifecycle
SEAL, ACTIVATE, RESOLVE and timeout VOID
Maintenance
CREATE and CLOSE
This keeps low-priority creation and teardown transactions from occupying the same wallet resources as boundary work. Different pools and lanes can progress concurrently, while actions spending the same PoolCell must serialize.
A shared database records lanes, pools, durable jobs, transaction attempts and resource leases. Workers revalidate chain state before spending. The indexer reconciles confirmations and exposes read APIs to the frontend.
Before broadcast, the executor persists the transaction hash and exact signed bytes. If submission returns an ambiguous response, it retains the reservation and reconciles that same transaction rather than assuming failure and building a conflicting replacement.
These mechanisms help recovery, but do not make the infrastructure fully independent: lanes still share the host, database, indexer and external services.
The backend does not choose a winning side by writing a result into its database. Settlement must satisfy the on-chain rules. However, operators still have availability responsibilities and control authorized sealing, timeout cancellation and teardown. This is not an operator-free system.
6. Using the application
Open turnmark.astromind.cc, connect a supported wallet and use its displayed CKB receiving address to fund it with testnet CKB.
The application includes:
A market view with the live indicative chart and entry ticket.
Positions, with active holdings and available claims or refunds.
Results for completed rounds.
A wallet panel with the CKB address, balance and CKB transfer flow.
A shared transaction tracker for signing, submission, confirmation and failure.
EVM wallets such as MetaMask connect through CCC. The wallet panel exposes the corresponding CKB address; the application still transacts on CKB testnet.
Some activity history is browser-local, rather than a complete account-wide historical index. Changing browser or origin does not carry that local history across.
7. What we have actually tested
On 13 November, we completed a funded public-testnet acceptance run covering one real 5-minute pool and one real 15-minute pool.
Each pool received one 1 CKB UP deposit and one 1 CKB DOWN deposit. Both finalized with UP as the winner. Winner redemptions and losing-share burns were confirmed, with each winner receiving the expected 1.98 CKB.
A separate read-only chain verification script checked:
All eight participant transactions, including exact signed bytes and witnesses.
The four exact start/end price proofs.
The consumed sealed cells and their ancestry to the signed checkpoints.
Payouts and zero remaining participant shares.
This was our own acceptance verification, not an external security audit.
The report is in docs/testnet-freeze-rails-acceptance-2026-11-13.md, with public evidence under docs/evidence/testnet-freeze-rails-2026-11-13/.
These two rounds demonstrate an end-to-end flow, not a reliability guarantee. Boundary submissions were acknowledged roughly 2.8–4.2 seconds after their boundaries; observed confirmations were roughly 20–62 seconds after them. Those measurements include different stages and should not be described as instant settlement.
8. Current limits
Testnet only. This is not a claim of mainnet readiness. Use faucet CKB.
One live oracle publisher. The current committee is 1-of-1. Threshold verification exists, but multiple independent operators are not yet providing the live trust model.
Larger committees need further work. The combined activation verifier measured about 112 million cycles at 7-of-9, exceeding the default 70-million-cycle transaction-pool verification limit. We cannot claim that increasing the committee is already a deployment-only change.
Claims have a finite window. Terminal pools can be torn down after a grace period measured from the scheduled close: eight times the round duration, bounded between one hour and seven days. That is one hour for 5m rounds and two hours for 15m rounds. Do not assume winnings or refunds remain claimable indefinitely. This policy deserves review before mainnet.
Refunds require transactions. A VOID outcome makes principal redeemable; it does not automatically send it back to every wallet. Transaction fees and capacity requirements still apply.
Infrastructure can delay progress. Oracle or RPC outages, shared-host failures and CKB confirmations affect availability. Separate wallet rails reduce one source of contention; they do not eliminate those dependencies.
More acceptance gates remain. Larger-quorum admission, xUDT pools, governance rotation, broader crash/contention testing and longer operational soak are still separate work.
9. What feedback would help
We would appreciate people trying a full testnet flow: connect, deposit, follow a round, then claim a win or refund. Tell us where the interface makes the rules or transaction status unclear.
For contract and protocol reviewers, we especially want scrutiny of:
Participation freezing and checkpoint trust assumptions.
Exact-boundary SPOT settlement and missing-price behavior.
Share accounting, payouts and refunds.
Operator authority, timeout behavior and claim-window policy.
Transaction recovery and conflicting-cell handling.
For product feedback: are 5m and 15m useful durations? Is the early deposit cutoff understandable? What would you need to see before trusting a market like this?
I will answer questions and share progress in this thread.

Turnmark lets you take a position on a simple question: will an asset’s price finish higher or lower over a fixed round?

We have BTC/USDT rounds running on Nervos testnet at two durations: 5 minutes and 15 minutes. You deposit test CKB into UP or DOWN before participation closes. The round compares committee-signed prices at its exact start and end boundaries. Winning shares can then be redeemed from the pool.

There is no order book and no house quoting odds. Participants on the two sides fund a shared pot. Your potential payout depends on how much is deposited on each side.

This is a working testnet application, not a mainnet launch. We are sharing it for people to try, review and help shape.

Try it: turnmark.astromind.cc — served over HTTPS.

Source: GitHub repository calledAdo/turnmark.

Addresses and repository paths are written as code here to avoid automatic links.

1. What a round looks like

Suppose a BTC/USDT round runs from 12:00 to 12:05:

  1. Before participation closes, choose UP or DOWN and deposit test CKB. You receive shares tied to that specific pool and side.
  2. Participation is sealed before 12:00. This gives the seal transaction time to confirm before the starting price becomes known.
  3. The exact signed 12:00 SPOT update supplies the starting price, provided the pool also has valid evidence that participation was frozen beforehand.
  4. The exact signed 12:05 SPOT update supplies the ending price.
  5. A higher ending price makes UP the winner. A lower price makes DOWN the winner. An exact tie makes stakes refundable.

The five-minute duration describes the price interval. It does not mean deposits stay open until 12:00, or that payouts are ready exactly at 12:05. Oracle availability, transaction submission and CKB confirmation are separate steps.

You can withdraw while the pool remains OPEN. Once it is sealed, participation is fixed.

How payouts work

This is a parimutuel market: winners recover their stake and share the losing side’s pot, after the configured fee on that losing pot.

For example, with 10 CKB on UP and 10 CKB on DOWN, a 2% fee, and an UP result:

  • The losing pot contributes 9.8 CKB after the 0.2 CKB fee.
  • UP holders share 19.8 CKB in proportion to their winning shares.
  • A participant holding 1 CKB of the 10 CKB UP stake receives 1.98 CKB, before their transaction costs.

The displayed payout is an estimate while deposits and withdrawals can still change the pot. It is not a fixed return. A losing position loses its stake.

2. What lives on CKB

The protocol uses CKB cells and four contracts:

Piece Responsibility
pool_type Validates pool state transitions, boundary-price evidence, accounting and settlement.
pool_admin_lock Separates lifecycle authority from creation and teardown authority.
share_xudt Represents pool-specific UP and DOWN shares and constrains minting and burning.
treasury_lock Guards the treasury used by the xUDT-backed pool path.

The public application currently uses CKB-backed pools. An xUDT path exists in the code, but the funded public-testnet acceptance described below does not establish that path’s readiness.

The core pool lifecycle is:

OPEN
  Deposits and withdrawals allowed
  |
  | SEAL participation before the start boundary
  v
SEALED
  Participation frozen
  |
  | ACTIVATE with exact start price + freeze proof
  v
LOCKED
  Round running
  |
  | RESOLVE with exact end price
  v
FINALIZED
  Winning shares redeemable

Cancellation paths:
  OPEN   -> VOID if empty or one-sided at seal, or on timeout
  SEALED -> VOID on activation timeout
  LOCKED -> VOID on resolution timeout

VOID: stakes refundable
Exact tie: refund outcome

An exact tie follows the refund outcome. After the claim grace period, an authorized maintenance transaction can consume the terminal PoolCell.

3. Why sealing and starting are separate

This is one of the most important parts of the design.

If deposits and the starting price were fixed in one transaction submitted at the boundary, that transaction might confirm after the price was already known. Participation could remain open too late.

Turnmark separates those events:

  • SEAL freezes participation ahead of the boundary.
  • ACTIVATE records the exact boundary price and verifies a signed checkpoint covering the actual sealed cell’s origin.

The checkpoint binds the network, boundary and accepted chain history. The contract checks the sealed cell’s origin and its header ancestry against that certificate.

There is an explicit trust limit: the committee attests to its external observation time and accepted chain cut. CKB headers alone cannot prove that something happened before a real-world wall-clock deadline.

Without acceptable freeze evidence, the pool must not start. The timeout path allows cancellation and refunds instead.

4. Where the prices come from

Turnmark uses Lean Oracle, introduced in the Nervos Talk post “Asset price oracle on Nervos Network” (topic 10800, at talk.nervos.org/t/asset-price-oracle-on-nervos-network/10800). That post explains the oracle’s publishers, signed updates and public mirror; this post focuses on how Turnmark uses them for prediction rounds.

Turnmark consumes the oracle through lean-oracle-sdk. Oracle publishers, price production and the public mirror run independently of this project’s workers.

For settlement, the pool pins its feed, exponent and publisher committee. ACTIVATE and RESOLVE verify the signed update directly, including quorum signatures and the feed’s Merkle inclusion proof. The live publisher-set cell is referenced as a read-only cell dependency.

The current product uses boundary SPOT, not TWAP:

  • Start price: the signed update whose timestamp exactly equals the configured start boundary.
  • End price: the signed update whose timestamp exactly equals the configured close boundary.
  • A later price is not substituted simply because the required update is unavailable.

The browser’s live chart is informational. It is not settlement evidence. The contract verifies the signed boundary update supplied in the transaction.

This also means oracle methodology matters. An exact signed SPOT tick proves what the committee signed; it does not make instantaneous markets immune to manipulation or guarantee a price will always be available.

5. What the backend does—and what it cannot do

Workers keep rounds moving. They create pools, seal participation, obtain boundary proofs, submit activation and resolution transactions, handle timeout cancellations and eventually clean up terminal pools.

Each asset-duration pair is a separate lane. BTC/USDT 5m and BTC/USDT 15m have their own schedules and worker services.

Within each lane, wallet responsibilities are split:

Rail Actions
Lifecycle SEAL, ACTIVATE, RESOLVE and timeout VOID
Maintenance CREATE and CLOSE

This keeps low-priority creation and teardown transactions from occupying the same wallet resources as boundary work. Different pools and lanes can progress concurrently, while actions spending the same PoolCell must serialize.

A shared database records lanes, pools, durable jobs, transaction attempts and resource leases. Workers revalidate chain state before spending. The indexer reconciles confirmations and exposes read APIs to the frontend.

Before broadcast, the executor persists the transaction hash and exact signed bytes. If submission returns an ambiguous response, it retains the reservation and reconciles that same transaction rather than assuming failure and building a conflicting replacement.

These mechanisms help recovery, but do not make the infrastructure fully independent: lanes still share the host, database, indexer and external services.

The backend does not choose a winning side by writing a result into its database. Settlement must satisfy the on-chain rules. However, operators still have availability responsibilities and control authorized sealing, timeout cancellation and teardown. This is not an operator-free system.

6. Using the application

Open turnmark.astromind.cc, connect a supported wallet and use its displayed CKB receiving address to fund it with testnet CKB.

The application includes:

  • A market view with the live indicative chart and entry ticket.
  • Positions, with active holdings and available claims or refunds.
  • Results for completed rounds.
  • A wallet panel with the CKB address, balance and CKB transfer flow.
  • A shared transaction tracker for signing, submission, confirmation and failure.

EVM wallets such as MetaMask connect through CCC. The wallet panel exposes the corresponding CKB address; the application still transacts on CKB testnet.

Some activity history is browser-local, rather than a complete account-wide historical index. Changing browser or origin does not carry that local history across.

7. What we have actually tested

On 13 November, we completed a funded public-testnet acceptance run covering one real 5-minute pool and one real 15-minute pool.

Each pool received one 1 CKB UP deposit and one 1 CKB DOWN deposit. Both finalized with UP as the winner. Winner redemptions and losing-share burns were confirmed, with each winner receiving the expected 1.98 CKB.

A separate read-only chain verification script checked:

  • All eight participant transactions, including exact signed bytes and witnesses.
  • The four exact start/end price proofs.
  • The consumed sealed cells and their ancestry to the signed checkpoints.
  • Payouts and zero remaining participant shares.

This was our own acceptance verification, not an external security audit.

The report is in docs/testnet-freeze-rails-acceptance-2026-11-13.md, with public evidence under docs/evidence/testnet-freeze-rails-2026-11-13/.

These two rounds demonstrate an end-to-end flow, not a reliability guarantee. Boundary submissions were acknowledged roughly 2.8–4.2 seconds after their boundaries; observed confirmations were roughly 20–62 seconds after them. Those measurements include different stages and should not be described as instant settlement.

8. Current limits

Testnet only. This is not a claim of mainnet readiness. Use faucet CKB.

One live oracle publisher. The current committee is 1-of-1. Threshold verification exists, but multiple independent operators are not yet providing the live trust model.

Larger committees need further work. The combined activation verifier measured about 112 million cycles at 7-of-9, exceeding the default 70-million-cycle transaction-pool verification limit. We cannot claim that increasing the committee is already a deployment-only change.

Claims have a finite window. Terminal pools can be torn down after a grace period measured from the scheduled close: eight times the round duration, bounded between one hour and seven days. That is one hour for 5m rounds and two hours for 15m rounds. Do not assume winnings or refunds remain claimable indefinitely. This policy deserves review before mainnet.

Refunds require transactions. A VOID outcome makes principal redeemable; it does not automatically send it back to every wallet. Transaction fees and capacity requirements still apply.

Infrastructure can delay progress. Oracle or RPC outages, shared-host failures and CKB confirmations affect availability. Separate wallet rails reduce one source of contention; they do not eliminate those dependencies.

More acceptance gates remain. Larger-quorum admission, xUDT pools, governance rotation, broader crash/contention testing and longer operational soak are still separate work.

9. What feedback would help

We would appreciate people trying a full testnet flow: connect, deposit, follow a round, then claim a win or refund. Tell us where the interface makes the rules or transaction status unclear.

For contract and protocol reviewers, we especially want scrutiny of:

  • Participation freezing and checkpoint trust assumptions.
  • Exact-boundary SPOT settlement and missing-price behavior.
  • Share accounting, payouts and refunds.
  • Operator authority, timeout behavior and claim-window policy.
  • Transaction recovery and conflicting-cell handling.

For product feedback: are 5m and 15m useful durations? Is the early deposit cutoff understandable? What would you need to see before trusting a market like this?

I will answer questions and share progress in this thread.

Thank you—your freshness question exposes a gap in how I explained the integration.
Comparing a price timestamp with an arbitrary header dep does not prevent an old price being paired with an old header. Our reference consumer binds the header to the block that created the input being spent and requires a later price. That proves “published after this input was created,” but does not establish freshness at liquidation time.
The consuming protocol defines its freshness requirements. for now, but we need to document precisely what each integration pattern guarantees. I’ll clarify that a header comparison alone is not a complete liquidation freshness solution.
I also agree on economic integrity. Committee signatures authenticate the reported price; they do not make the underlying markets manipulation-proof. Exposure caps, confidence/deviation checks and spot/TWAP cross-checks are appropriate consumer safeguards, particularly for the thinner CKB markets. Our historical manipulation-cost estimates should be treated as measurements from that dataset, not guaranteed security bounds.

Thank you—yes, the publishers already check proposal timestamps against their own clocks before signing. They reject ticks outside a configured signing window, and separately enforce when the proposer’s slot opens. A far-future proposal from a faulty leader should therefore be rejected by correctly clocked honest signers.
However, the current price_feed_type does not independently enforce an upper timestamp bound against a header dep. Your failure scenario is valid if a far-future quorum-signed update reaches the feed cell: the strictly-newer rule would reject subsequent ordinary timestamps. Rotating the committee alone would not reset that cell’s timestamp.
An on-chain upper bound is a sensible additional safeguard. I’ll investigate it with explicit header-reference rules and regression tests. It would address future-timestamp poisoning, while old-price/old-header freshness remains a separate consumer integration concern. Since the deployed contracts are immutable, introducing this protection would require a new deployment and integrator migration; it is not a guarantee the current contract provides.

Hi @TolgaYazan,
Thank you for taking the time to prepare and submit the proposal, and for documenting the existing MVP in detail.
The committee has completed its review and, after careful discussion, regrets to reject the secnev proposal at this time.
We want to be candid about the reasons for this decision:
Outside the scope of the Spark Program: The core incremental work that Spark funding would support—tracking the state of the Stable++ protocol (that is, the collateral, oracle, and redemption health behind RUSD)—is outside the Spark Program’s funding scope.
Focused on an unsuitable layer: We recognize the value of the product’s market risk analysis features (real-time cell data, holder concentration, wallet exposure, and dCKB transaction replay). However, a substantial portion of the proposed work concerns Stable++’s internal protocol state. The committee believes this work would be better suited to the Community Fund DAO or direct collaboration with the Stable++ team, rather than Spark support.
We appreciate your team’s efforts to build a working MVP on mainnet, and recognize the work behind the real-time dashboard and cell-level data infrastructure. You have clearly laid a solid technical foundation.
We truly appreciate all the effort your team has put in. Please keep building, and feel free to reach out anytime!
Best regards

2026 November 17, Eighth Weekly Report
Recognition is the first step toward improvement. Decentralization does not automatically guarantee reliability and stability. This became clearly evident when we encountered several practical obstacles during the implementation of a network node that was originally intended to be as stable and reliably accessible as possible. The network connection experienced a prolonged outage on the provider’s end. From 7:50 p.m. local time on November 10, 2026, until 11:30 a.m. the following day. After that, the payment system for the volume-based quota payments I had selected did not work until early afternoon the next day.
The volume-based quota solution was chosen as a workaround to avoid the high one-time payment required for an account with unlimited traffic. This proves to be a good and fast connection when data usage is low. In this regard, bypassing the unlimited data plan by using the volume-based plan has proven to be a sensible option. However, we have so far avoided conducting IDB tests on boot nodes via this method. These initial block downloads are the first thing new nodes do on the network. The IDB takes several hours, depending on the performance of the hardware and the network connection.
As I said, acknowledging the problem is the first step toward improvement, and so the Atlantic node will, for the time being, be a full node that contributes to the global diversity of transaction distribution, but it will not be a permanently accessible boot node.
A VPN connection to a local Internet service provider with a static residential IP address already exists; however, this provider is located in Germany, in Central Europe, and therefore offers little geographic diversity. Nevertheless, a node there would provide further diversification away from data centers and would benefit from very good Internet and power availability. Outages there have been extremely rare in the past. Furthermore, there are currently no full nodes in that locally restricted IP address range. Operating a community-managed boot node there is far more realistic than here on the West African islands. This static IP address is already available and can be used as needed; this will not change in the foreseeable future.
The experience we have gained with Qubes OS will help us operate a stable boot node. Given the current situation—with occasional internet and power outages, no static IP address, and a limited data allowance—the question arises as to whether it would make more sense to use a more pragmatic system that is easier to manage and offers greater flexibility in usage.
It is supposed to be optimized for operation as a full node, which is how we came across CachyOS, which offers architecture-optimized kernel builds.
CachyOS is a performance-optimized Arch Linux distribution with CPU-specific package builds and advanced kernel scheduling.
Unlike Qubes OS, where most of the hardware is available to dom0 and other app-Qubes are severely restricted until the hardware is explicitly passed to them. We recognize the opportunities presented by programs that will use or are already using Nervos Network. And we are limited to full-node operation; therefore, we will not be operating a boot node in West Africa for the foreseeable future. As a result, we are currently considering whether to discontinue this highly secure but severely restricted operation and repurpose the hardware for a local full node by implementing a different system, such as Arch Linux rolling release model “CachyOS”.
Regardless of this consideration and observation, operations on Qubes OS are currently continuing, barring external circumstances beyond our control.
To ensure these settings remain in effect after reboots, we have entered the following lines in Qube sys-net:
sudo tee /rw/config/qubes-firewall-user-script >/dev/null <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
nft add chain qubes custom-dnat-port8115 '{ type nat hook prerouting priority filter +1 ; policy accept; }'
nft add rule qubes custom-dnat-port8115 iifname "ens7" tcp dport 8115 ct state new,established,related counter dnat 10.138.4.97
nft add rule qubes custom-forward iifname "ens7" ip daddr 10.138.4.97 tcp dport 8115 ct state new,established,related counter accept
EOF
sudo chmod +x /rw/config/qubes-firewall-user-script
This saves the three rules and makes the script executable. Then we check whether the three rules are present in the file:
sudo cat /rw/config/qubes-firewall-user-script
Now we add the following rule to the App-Qube where our CKB Nervos node is running and make the script executable:
sudo tee -a /rw/config/qubes-firewall-user-script >/dev/null <<'EOF'
nft add rule qubes custom-input tcp dport 8115 ip daddr 10.137.0.7 ct state new,established,related counter accept
EOF
sudo chmod +x /rw/config/qubes-firewall-user-script
Then we again check whether the rule is present:
sudo cat /rw/config/qubes-firewall-user-script
Sys-Firewall turned out to be a special Qube where the standard “default-dvm” template must be cloned and switched to in order to make changes persistent. Unfortunately, this caused us some problems, so we settled on the pragmatic solution of manually entering the firewall rules into the Sys-Firewall console after every reboot.
sudo nft add chain qubes custom-dnat-port8115 '{ type nat hook prerouting priority filter +1 ; policy accept; }'
sudo nft add rule qubes custom-dnat-port8115 iifgroup 1 tcp dport 8115 ct state new,established,related counter dnat 10.137.0.7
sudo nft add rule qubes custom-forward iifgroup 1 ip daddr 10.137.0.7 tcp dport 8115 ct state new,established,related counter accept
Consequently, only the sys-firewall rules are not persistent and must be re-entered with every reboot. We have found this effort to be acceptable, and so we have not yet investigated the issues related to cloning and reactivating this default template any further.
As a test, the system has already been configured with bootnode = true in the ckb.toml file to achieve greater diversity in logged connections. Those node IDs that are unique to their country at the time of verification deserve a spot on our node’s whitelist. The system is currently running with a limit of 20 connections and the default setting of 125 peers. So far, we don’t have many unique country nodes on the whitelist. Two of them are regular official boot nodes: Santiago, South America, and Cape Town, South Africa.
Even though this weekly report may sound like a setback, it might actually be an important step in the right direction: Geographic diversification is already in place through the operation of this full node, and we aren’t rigidly clinging to something that has proven difficult to sustain. Instead, we’re moving forward where we want to make progress: We’re collecting a highly diverse range of node IDs and IP addresses in our node’s whitelist and keeping it up to date to keep things running.
./ckb run

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | ckb-msig: check and merge CKB multisig signatures from ckb-cli, Neuron and CCC
recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @ILE_LABS,
Thank you for taking the time to prepare and submit the ckb-msig proposal, and for the thoughtful revision based on our earlier feedback.
The committee has completed its review and, after careful discussion, regrets to reject the ckb-msig proposal at this time.
We want to be transparent about the reasoning behind this decision:
The core problem remains unsolved: The proposal’s solution does not fully address the underlying coordination bottleneck in multisig workflows. While ckb-msig can check, merge, and convert signatures across formats, the fundamental issue persists — after using these tools, signers must still collect all signatures and forward them to a single individual for aggregation. In other words, it automates the validation and formatting of signatures, but the awkward manual step of gathering, forwarding, and coordinating remains. We are not convinced this meaningfully improves the multisig signing experience in practice.
Valuable insight, but wrong direction: We acknowledge the prototype’s utility in reconciling signature formats between ckb-cli, Neuron, and CCC. However, rather than building a tool that adapts to the existing fragmentation, we believe the more impactful contribution would be to design and propose a unified standard for multisig signature formats — one that ckb-cli, Neuron, CCC, and other tools would collectively adopt. This would address the root issue so that signatures are inherently interoperable, and no “middle-layer” bridging tool is needed.
The committee acknowledges your team’s effort and capabilities demonstrated through the prototype, and we appreciate ILE Labs’ commitment to the CKB ecosystem. Should you be interested in pursuing the unified format standard direction in the future, we would welcome a new application.
Thank you very much for all the hard work your team has put in. Keep building, and feel free to reach out anytime!
Best,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
Since 2023, 178 people have voted in the Community Fund DAO, about 1% of the 16,610 Nervos DAO depositors. We wanted to understand why more holders do not take part, and found one reason that can be fixed: 1,132 depositors can only vote if they move their deposit to Neuron first, because the wallet they use cannot bind today. Other reasons need asking, so there is a short poll at the end.
Read from CKB mainnet at block 21,038,015 and from Metaforo’s public API, both on 2026-11-17, read only. We build Ward and the Cellula wallet and had a proposal in this DAO (t/11089, passed on 16 November), so we waited for its vote to close before posting this. The scripts and raw data are available to anyone who wants to check them.
How a vote is counted today
Metaforo binds a CKB address with a message signed the way Neuron signs (secp256k1), which is how most people held CKB when the DAO started. A vote weighs the Nervos DAO deposits under the bound addresses. All 614 addresses bound by the 178 people who have ever voted are secp256k1 addresses. Logging in with JoyID works, but deposits under the JoyID address are not counted.
1. Who votes
39 votes since February 2023. The median vote had 15 voters and 1.2% of the DAO’s deposits on its closing day (94.0M CKB; 155.0M over the last 12 months). The highest were 50 voters (Rosen Bridge integration, January 2026) and 7.3% of deposits (Community Fund DAO v1.1, November 2025).
178 people have ever voted, 81 of them in the last 12 months. The addresses voters bound hold 980.0M CKB in deposits today, 12.0% of the DAO.
2. Who cannot vote from their own wallet
Live Nervos DAO deposits: 8,179,234,336 CKB under 16,610 locks (the explorer shows the same two numbers). By the lock that holds them:

Deposits outside secp256k1 cannot be bound today: 1,132 depositors with 390.0M CKB (4.8%). Portal Wallet had a path in 2023 (t/7053), but none of the 614 bound addresses is a PW-lock. Leaving PW-lock aside, it is 206 depositors with 230.8M CKB (2.8%). Some voters already log in with JoyID; deposits under their JoyID addresses are not counted today.
These wallets use the DAO more than most: JoyID holders keep 37% of their CKB in deposits, PW-lock 56%, Omnilock 31%, the quantum-resistant lock 49%. For secp256k1 addresses it is about 16% (approximate, see the limits).
The wallet is not the main reason people do not vote: about 15,000 depositors can bind today and have not. Why, the chain cannot say.
3. The 30 day lock
Weight needs the CKB in the DAO, and leaving it takes up to about 30 days. How many holders stay out for that reason, the chain cannot tell either: most of the CKB outside the DAO (about 41.7B) sits with exchanges, team and foundation addresses. 843.2M CKB is in phase 1 of a withdrawal right now.
Counting any wallet
Counting deposits from any lock would let the 1,132 depositors above vote from the wallet they already use. One way is a lock proof, which we have been building as Ward (GitHub - LusoCryptoLabs/ckb-ward: Ward: lock proof for CKB. Prove control of any CKB lock with a proof transaction that can never land on chain. · GitHub); votes signed by the deposit’s own lock, as in ckb-treasury-lab, are another. We are happy to help with either.

What is the main reason?
I did not know about these votes
My wallet cannot bind (JoyID, MetaMask, UniSat, OKX, other)
Binding and voting take too much effort
My CKB is on an exchange
I do not want it locked in the Nervos DAO
My vote would not change the result
Other (please reply)
0
voters
Method and limits
Deposits: every live cell with the Nervos DAO type at block 21,038,015 (indexer get_cells); data of 8 zero bytes is a deposit, anything else a withdrawal in progress.
Lock kinds from CCC’s list of mainnet scripts; the Omnilock mode from the first byte of its args; the quantum-resistant lock and iCKB identified by code hash.
Votes, bound addresses, login keys and each voter’s weight from Metaforo’s public API (39 polls, 178 voter profiles). Shares use the explorer’s daily DAO total on each closing day.
A depositor here is a distinct lock. One person can hold several, and an exchange can hold many people’s CKB under one. Large voters are not identified.
The total held by secp256k1 addresses is circulating supply less the other lock families, because the public indexer timed out adding up every secp256k1 cell. That makes the 16% approximate.

recent_posts.author: tun_tunn03
recent_posts.content_text:
I replayed recent CKB mainnet transactions in ckb-debugger, one run per script group, to see where the cycles go. Every transaction is checked against the node: the groups have to add up exactly to the cycles the node recorded for it, or the transaction is listed as excluded instead of counted.
There are two samples, kept apart on purpose.
A random sample: every non-cellbase transaction in every 12th block from 20,932,885 to 20,946,673 (5 Nov 12:54 to 7 Nov 04:00 UTC, about 39 hours). 1,002 transactions, all 1,002 matched the node, nothing excluded.
Script Groups Median p90 Share
secp256k1_blake160 (lock) 1,002 1,647,946 1,665,060 71.9%
unknown 0xa9267ff5...e981 (type) 175 1,801,237 1,836,377 13.7%
Type ID (type) 175 1,000,000 1,000,000 7.6%
Bitcoin SPV client, RGB++ (type) 33 1,366,700 1,551,628 2.0%
d.id time oracle, info (type) 648 45,174 45,175 1.3%
JoyID (lock) 4 6,833,689 6,862,057 1.2%
d.id time oracle, index (type) 648 32,977 32,977 0.9%
4 unknown locks (see below) 175 each 4,426 to 72,371 1.3%
Nervos DAO (type) 11 11,981 14,084 <0.01%
Per transaction: median 1,729,190 cycles, p90 4,607,770, max 6,865,540.
A targeted sample. The random window has few or no xUDT, Omnilock or Spore transactions, so for 22 scripts I asked the node’s indexer for the most recent transactions in which each one ran (searching back from block 20,947,093, up to 3,000,000 blocks for the rare ones) and replayed up to 40 of each. 650 replays: 604 matched the node, none mismatched, and 46 older transactions (all at or before block 19,011,137) have no cycle total on the public node, so they are listed as not recorded rather than counted. These were picked by script, so they say what a script costs when it runs, not how much of mainnet it is. No shares here.
Script (per group) Matched groups Median p90
xUDT 41 20,564 20,717
Omnilock, Ethereum displaying 37 1,460,165 1,476,761
Omnilock, Bitcoin 40 1,458,571 1,472,092
JoyID 40 6,815,869 6,879,521
Spore 40 105,299 272,482
Spore Cluster 40 98,683 122,630
ckb-dex lock 39 24,267 39,032
RGB++ lock 1,444 1,418,522 1,419,245
BTC time lock (RGB++) 9 813,924 959,098
COTA 49 2,332,001 2,332,001
iCKB limit order 40 75,304 79,679
iCKB logic 8 105,870 160,850
anyone-can-pay 40 34,106 1,609,984
sUDT 20 5,540 32,871
d.id das-lock 61 282,271 3,862,283
Nervos DAO 40 11,974 13,826
Type ID 40 1,000,000 1,000,000
What I take from it:
Most of mainnet’s verification cost is still the default lock: secp256k1_blake160 is 71.9% of all cycles in this window, 1.60M to 1.67M per group for 90% of them. It runs once per distinct owner, so a transaction that spends cells of many owners costs that many times more. There was no such transaction in this window (the costliest was 6,865,540 cycles); in a window I measured on 28 Oct, one with 68 owners cost 111,979,599.
648 of the 1,002 random transactions are d.id’s time oracle updating its timestamp and block number cells. The two type scripts are cheap (about 45k and 33k); the cost of those transactions is the lock.
175 transactions follow one pattern I cannot name yet: secp256k1_blake160, a Type ID cell, a type script with code hash 0xa9267ff5…e981 at about 1.8M cycles, and four small locks (4,426 to 72,371 cycles). About 4.61M cycles per transaction. Their code cells were deployed in October 2021 and June 2022, so this is not a new protocol. It was in the targeted Type ID sample on 28 Oct as well (26 of 40), but not in that random window.
Type scripts are cheap next to locks. xUDT runs at about 20k cycles, Spore and Cluster around 100k, sUDT under 33k. In an xUDT transfer the lock is most of the bill: the commonest xUDT pattern in the sample was JoyID plus xUDT (16 of 40), at a median of 6,851,229 cycles for the whole transaction, against 1,677,720 for secp256k1 plus xUDT.
Locks vary a lot. Omnilock in Ethereum or Bitcoin mode is about 1.46M, close to secp256k1. JoyID is about 6.8M per group, four times that. The RGB++ lock is about 1.42M per group, but RGB++ transactions spend many cells with distinct args: 36 of the 40 sampled RGB++ transactions ran 40 RGB++ lock groups each and cost about 57M cycles.
Type ID shows exactly 1,000,000 because the node verifies it natively and charges a fixed amount; the tools charge the same.
I made the same measurement on 28 Oct with an older version of the tool. 389 transactions are in both runs (mostly in the targeted samples), and every one gave the same cycles for every group. So the differences between the two reports come from which transactions were on chain in each window, not from the tool.
The full report (min, median, p90 and max for each script, an example transaction, the cell each script’s code was loaded from, what ran together, and every excluded transaction with its reason): ckb-cycle-tools/atlas/2026-11-07/report.md at main · luongthanhtung03/ckb-cycle-tools · GitHub
The raw per-transaction, per-group results are in data.json next to it. The 28 Oct run is still there for comparison: ckb-cycle-tools/atlas/2026-10-28/report.md at main · luongthanhtung03/ckb-cycle-tools · GitHub
How it is measured: ckb-cycle-tools rebuilds each transaction as a ckb-debugger mock transaction from the node (input cells, cell deps with dep groups expanded, header deps) and runs each script group on the CKB-VM version of its block. Script names come from CCC’s known scripts plus a short table of code hashes published elsewhere (Spore and Cluster in @ckb-ccc/spore, RGB++ in rgbpp-sdk, d.id in its own repositories, iCKB’s deployment file, the ckb-dex SDK), each with its source next to it. Scripts with no published hash stay “unknown”. To reproduce the random sample:
npm ci
npm run atlas -- --rpc https://mainnet.ckb.dev/ --to 20946673 --blocks 13789 --stride 12 --max-txs 1002
The command for the targeted samples is at the end of the report; --script takes a script name or any code hash, so you can point it at your own script.
The numbers do not depend on the debugger release. 24 recorded transactions (22 mainnet, one for each script sampled above, and 2 testnet) were replayed under 16 ckb-debugger builds, every release from 0.121.0 to 1.1.2 (16 Nov), native and WebAssembly. Every build gave the same cycles for every group: ckb-cycle-tools/compat/RESULTS.md at main · luongthanhtung03/ckb-cycle-tools · GitHub

Two questions for anyone who knows mainnet traffic better than I do:
24 scripts in these transactions are still unknown to me, among them the 0xa9267ff5…e981 type script and the four locks from point 3. The report shows each one’s code hash (shortened; the full hashes are in data.json) next to the scripts it ran with. If you know one and can point to where its code hash is published, I will name it.

recent_posts.author: PANAGOT
recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks @ding99bt @xingtianchunyan. Links work for me now. Full proposal per the Spark template:
1. Project Overview
Name: TalkDID
One-liner: Discourse plugin that binds Nervos Talk accounts to did:ckb and shows a Verified did:ckb badge on profiles/posts.
Type: OSS Discourse plugin (app-layer)
Demo: https://talkdid-ckb-j9kz.vercel.app/
2. Team
Independent full-stack builder: Panagiotis Pollis (PANAGOT / panagot)
12+ years in cryptocurrency. Already shipped the Live CCC challenge/sign/verify demo + Discourse UI preview + plugin stub in this repo.
Twitter / X : PANAGOT
3. Why this project exists
The Spark committee previously recommended Discourse + CKB DID as a higher-adoption direction than another DID tutorial:
Spark Program | DID Quickstart Kit — Practical DID Consumption Demo Spark Program
Hi @Carl,
Thank you for taking the time to join Spark Program.
The committee has completed its review and, after careful discussion, regrets to Reject the DID Quickstart Kit projn at this time.
We want to be transparent about the reasoning behind this decision:
Lack of genuine demand for a DID creation tutorial:
Currently, the CKB ecosystem does not show a significant need for a dedicated “quickstart” guide focused solely on DID creation. The existing production apps (xjdao.xyz, bbs.fans…
TalkDID implements that recommendation: native CKB identity verification on Nervos Talk itself.
Nervos Talk accounts today are ordinary Discourse logins. did:ckb already works elsewhere (Vellum, CCC did-ckb, Metaforo/DAO, bbs.fans). On Talk, wallet/DID claims still rely on screenshots and social trust.
4. Solution
TalkDID is a reusable Discourse plugin + Theme Component that consumes existing did:ckb / CCC tooling (does not rebuild Vellum or Metaforo).
User flow:
User is logged into Talk and connects a CKB wallet via CCC
Server issues a cryptographically random, single-use challenge bound to that Discourse user + short TTL
Wallet signs the challenge
Server verifies the signature, resolves did:ckb (via @ckb-ccc/did-ckb patterns), and only then writes the bind
A Verified did:ckb badge appears on profile and posts
Unlink / re-link supported (re-link requires a fresh successful verify)
Trust model: The badge means this Discourse account proved control of that did:ckb at verification time. It does not mean KYC, real-world identity, or that the user is trustworthy.
Storage: Bind is written server-side to a protected UserCustomField only after successful verify. Users cannot self-assign a verified badge by editing profile fields.
Adoption path: MIT plugin reusable by Nervos Talk (if admins opt in) and other CKB Discourse communities.
5. Technical Approach
Discourse plugin (Ruby) + Theme Component + CCC / @ckb-ccc/did-ckb.
Trust boundary: Discourse session ≠ DID proof.
Challenge rules: random nonce · bound to authenticated user · short expiry · single-use · reject invalid / expired / replayed signatures · no bind on DID resolve failure.
Verify via Docker Dev Discourse (no need to install on talk.nervos.org to review).
6. Plan (2 weeks)
Week 1 (M1): Auth + DID bind + negative tests + Docker Dev docs
Week 2 (M2): Badge UI + unlink/re-link + verify pack + Spark update post
7. Funding
Ask: $500 · Spark 20%/80%
M1 — $250 — Working auth + DID bind
Acceptance:
Valid signature accepted; invalid signature rejected
Expired and replayed challenges rejected
DID association stored only after successful verify
Automated tests for the above + Docker Dev README
M2 — $250 — Badge + verify pack
Acceptance:
Verified did:ckb badge on profile and posts
Unlink removes badge; re-link requires fresh verify
MIT; Spark update post
8. Deliverables + Verify
Ship: MIT plugin + Theme Component · Docker Dev README · tests · verify GIF/checklist · Spark update post
9. Current vs funded
Now: live CCC companion kit + plugin stub (honest scaffold).
Spark funds: production-shaped challenge/verify/bind, badge UI, reproducible Docker Dev verify pack.
The Vite kit is the proposal companion; the funded artifact is the installable plugin.
10. CKB alignment
Uses existing did:ckb + CCC on Nervos Talk (Spark’s own venue). App-layer adoption of infrastructure the ecosystem already has — not a new protocol feature.

Update: I’ve reviewed the deliverables. The first thing I noticed is that users have to generate/provide two secp256k1 private keys (one for owner and one for recipient) in order to use Tranfr. I believe this would create a significant gap between daily users with the Tranfr protocol. Notice that, in order to use Tranfr, users have to use wallets specifically adapted for Tranfr.
I would recommend modifying this part in the protocol and allowing verification of users’ identity with any wallets. A possible solution, besides integrating all signing algorithms into the protocol, is to require a cell with our desired lock to be unlocked within the same transaction (like a self-transfer, but with no need to check the output).

recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks, for the feedback. I’ll remove in-script signature verification and delegate authorization to the owner’s and recipient’s own locks, as you suggested.
New design: the args hold the owner lock hash, the recipient lock hash and the deadline. The owner path is valid when the transaction spends an input locked by the owner’s lock. The recipient path is valid when the transaction spends an input locked by the recipient’s lock and every Tranfr input’s absolute since has reached the deadline. The lock verifies no signatures, so any wallet or lock type can be owner or recipient, and the SDK takes a signer callback instead of private keys. The typed-cell refund rule stays as is.
One question: I’d like to use 20-byte lock-hash prefixes, as Cheque does, which makes the args 48 bytes and the minimum cell capacity 89 CKB. Is that fine with you?
I’ll redeploy and re-record the testnet lifecycle, including a run with a non-secp256k1 lock.

recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] CKB × NEAR Intents: Building a Cross-Chain Bridge and Multichain Swap Gateway
recent_posts.author: asondev
recent_posts.content_text:
[DIS] CKB × NEAR Intents: Building a Cross-Chain Bridge and Multichain Swap Gateway
Funding Requested: 7,000 USDT equivalent
Estimated Duration: 8 weeks
Applicant / Team: FoundationLab
GitHub: ckbswap
1. Executive Summary
This project proposes building a bridge between CKB and NEAR and integrating with NEAR Intents to create a gateway for exchanging CKB across blockchain ecosystems.
Users will be able to bridge CKB to NEAR, receive its bridged representation, nCKB, and exchange it for a target asset through an intent-based swap flow. In the reverse direction, users will be able to exchange supported assets for nCKB and redeem it for native CKB.
The project will cover architecture, bridge contracts, MPC signing, relayer services, Intents integration, a reference quoting service, a user interface, and testing documentation. The deliverable will be a reproducible testnet prototype demonstrating the complete bridge-and-swap lifecycle.
We request 7,000 USDT equivalent from the CKB Community Fund DAO to complete this work over 8 weeks, establishing the technical foundation for future mainnet integration and liquidity partnerships.
2. Background and Motivation
Expanding CKB’s adoption requires making it easier for users from other ecosystems to acquire and use CKB, while giving CKB holders access to a broader range of assets and applications.
A bridge enables asset transfers between networks. An exchange integration addresses the next question: what can users do with those assets after bridging?
This project combines both capabilities:
Native CKB → nCKB on NEAR → NEAR Intents settlement → Target asset
The reverse path will be:
Source asset → NEAR Intents settlement → nCKB → Native CKB redemption
NEAR Intents provides infrastructure for expressing desired outcomes, obtaining quotes, and settling exchanges. Its documentation describes cross-chain swap interfaces and custom contract integrations. NEAR Intents documentation
By connecting CKB to this infrastructure, the project aims to reduce the friction of entering and leaving the CKB ecosystem and make CKB more accessible to multichain users and applications.
3. Project Objectives
Build a bidirectional CKB–NEAR bridge
Implement CKB deposits, nCKB issuance on NEAR, nCKB burning, and withdrawals back to CKB.
nCKB will follow the NEP-141 token standard and use a reserve accounting model designed around 1 nCKB representing 1 CKB. Deposit, issuance, withdrawal, and reserve reconciliation rules will be documented publicly.
Enable intent-based nCKB swaps
Implement the integration needed to deposit nCKB into an Intents settlement contract, query balances, obtain quotes, sign swap intents, execute settlement, and withdraw assets.
This phase will include a reference quoting and execution service that demonstrates bidirectional swaps between nCKB and at least one test asset in a controlled environment.
Provide a unified user interface
Users will be able to view deposit addresses, select a swap direction, review quotes and fees, and track bridge and swap progress through one interface.
Establish a foundation for broader CKB distribution
Publish reusable interfaces and documentation for future integrations with wallets, aggregators, and cross-chain applications.
The initial scope focuses on native CKB. Support for additional CKB ecosystem assets will be evaluated separately based on demand, security requirements, and liquidity availability.
4. Product and Technical Design
CKB-to-NEAR deposits
Users deposit CKB into designated addresses. After the configured number of confirmations, an authorized relayer submits the deposit record to the NEAR bridge contract, which processes nCKB issuance.
Deposits will be identified by transaction hash and output index to prevent duplicate processing and associate each deposit with its recipient and amount.
NEAR-to-CKB withdrawals
Users submit withdrawal requests, and the bridge contract handles nCKB burning and withdrawal state.
The system will use NEAR Chain Signatures to request MPC signatures for CKB withdrawal transactions. The contract will validate recipient amounts and change destinations, while the relayer handles broadcasting, confirmation tracking, and status updates.
NEAR Intents integration
After bridging, nCKB can enter an intent-based exchange flow. A reference execution service will provide quotes and submit compatible execution intents alongside the user’s signed intent.
The testing environment will use the open-source NEAR Intents Verifier contract and test assets to validate actual contract settlement. Project-operated test deployments will be clearly distinguished from production services. NEAR Intents contracts
The project will also prepare asset integration information, quoting interfaces, and liquidity requirements for future production integration.
Public nCKB swaps will require execution providers willing to quote and supply liquidity. Issuing a bridged token does not automatically make it available across the public swap network. NEAR Intents’ asset onboarding guidance identifies liquidity and solver coordination as part of this process. Token onboarding guidance
User interface
A lightweight web application will support:
Wallet connection, CKB deposit addresses, and balance viewing.
Deposits, swaps, and CKB redemption.
Quotes, minimum received amounts, fees, and quote expiry.
Deposit confirmation, settlement, and withdrawal tracking.
Transaction history and block explorer links.
Clear handling of unavailable quotes, expired quotes, and service errors.
5. Value to the CKB Ecosystem
Broader access to CKB. The project will establish a technical route for users from other ecosystems to acquire CKB with fewer manual steps.
More opportunities to use CKB. CKB holders will gain a foundation for accessing other assets and applications through a unified flow, supporting future payment and cross-chain use cases.
New liquidity connections. Intents-based quoting and execution can create opportunities to connect CKB with external market makers and asset networks. Actual depth and pricing will depend on liquidity participation.
Greater ecosystem visibility. Open-source integrations, demonstrations, and developer documentation will introduce CKB to more NEAR and multichain developers and reduce future integration work.
Reusable public infrastructure. The funded work will include bridge contracts, signing adapters, relayers, Intents integration, and a reference interface that other teams can inspect and reuse.
Success will be measured through verifiable software deliverables rather than speculative promises about users, trading volume, or total value locked.
6. Development Plan and Acceptance Criteria

Timeline

Acceptance Criteria

M1: Architecture and integration design
Weeks 1–2
Bridge architecture, asset flows, permission model, Intents interfaces, and liquidity plan
Publish the design, including quoting, settlement, fees, and failure handling

Settlement integration, reference quoting service, and user interface

M4: Verification and public delivery

Failure testing, fixes, documentation, demonstration, and final report

Total

Testing will cover duplicate deposits, unauthorized calls, invalid withdrawal outputs, quote expiry, slippage limits, replay protection, signing failures, and relayer restarts.
A public mainnet swap service requires additional security review, asset onboarding, and production liquidity. Third-party listing or launch commitments are outside this phase’s acceptance criteria.
7. Budget and Disbursement
Budget Item

Bidirectional bridge contracts and deposit/withdrawal relayers

Disbursement is proposed upon acceptance of each milestone. The budget and milestone tables describe the same funding allocation and are not additive.
The request is denominated in USDT equivalent. The payment asset and conversion method will follow the DAO’s approved arrangement.
This budget covers development and test delivery. It does not include mainnet liquidity capital, trading incentives, a formal third-party security audit, or ongoing production operations.
8. Security and Operational Boundaries
This phase will use authorized relayers to report CKB deposits. The trust assumptions will be disclosed, with permission controls, pause functionality, and processing limits.
MPC provides distributed signing. It does not replace deposit verification, bridge contract security, or administrative controls.
Withdrawal transactions will be checked for recipient, amount, and change destination. Complete on-chain enforcement of miner fees requires trustworthy input information.
Bridging and swapping involve multiple execution steps. Atomic settlement within the Intents contract does not make the entire cross-chain journey atomic. Each stage will have separate tracking and documented recovery procedures.
Swaps will require valid quotes, minimum received amounts, expiry conditions, and replay protection. Unavailable quotes will prevent execution.
A withdrawal that has already received a valid signature cannot be refunded solely because it timed out: the signed transaction might still be broadcast. Recovery procedures must prevent duplicate payouts.
The funded release is a testnet prototype. Mainnet deployment, formal external auditing, light-client or SPV deposit verification, and a complete multi-relayer consensus system are outside this phase.
9. Open Source, Maintenance, and Community Updates
Source code, tests, deployment scripts, and documentation will be published under a clearly specified open-source license, respecting dependency licenses.
Progress updates will be published every two weeks. Final delivery will include:
Deployable bridge and Intents integration code.
A testnet interface and demonstration video.
Deposit, swap, and withdrawal records.
A test report, deployment guide, and security documentation.
Asset integration materials and production liquidity requirements.
Long-term operations and mainnet maintenance will require a separate ownership and funding arrangement.
10. Funding Request
We request 7,000 USDT equivalent to build a bidirectional CKB–NEAR bridge and demonstrate asset exchange through NEAR Intents.
The goal is to establish a multichain gateway for CKB: making it easier for external users to acquire CKB, enabling CKB holders to access more assets and applications, and expanding CKB’s reach through open, reusable integrations.

topics.title: Spark Program | Lifeboat: see what an address owns on CKB, and get it out when the app is gone

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | Lifeboat: see what an address owns on CKB, and get it out when the app is gone
recent_posts.author: ding99bt
recent_posts.content_text:
1. Project Overview
Name: Lifeboat
One line: a static web app that scans a CKB address (or an old MetaMask address) and, where the holder can act alone, builds the exit transaction for assets whose wallet, bridge or app is gone.
Problem it solves:
Wallets, bridges and apps on CKB shut down: Portal Wallet, Godwoken, Force Bridge, USDI, NexisDAO.
Their users’ assets usually stay on chain, under scripts the holder can often still satisfy. What disappears is the website that knew how to build the transaction.
Lifeboat shows what an address really holds. Where the holder can act alone, it builds that transaction and shows it in full before the holder signs it in their own wallet.
Who uses it:
CKB holders who used an old wallet or app and are not sure what is left: one paste of an address, nothing to install, nothing signed.
Reviewers and the community, through a public sheet that says, protocol by protocol, whether a holder can get out without the team.
Type: user safety / resilience tool, open source (MIT).
Repository: GitHub - ding99bt/lifeboat · GitHub
Live demo: https://lifeboat-ckb.vercel.app
What already exists: a working scanner on mainnet and testnet, a Nervos DAO exit verified end to end on a local devnet, a “Left behind” table built from the CKB Explorer, and 24 unit tests.
What Spark adds: the Portal Wallet move-out, reclaiming CKB from dead token cells, an exit sheet for about 10 protocols, a full testnet cycle with real wallets and 10 user sessions, and a static release on IPFS.

What is built today, and what this grant funds.
Live product screenshots
image1920×1200 318 KB
Home page. Read-only demo: nothing is signed on mainnet.
image2560×2512 347 KB
Pasting the Ethereum address once used with Portal Wallet: Lifeboat derives its pw-lock and finds 50,000 CKB under a discontinued product. Addresses are blurred in this screenshot.
image2368×1490 316 KB
A JoyID wallet with several kinds of cells, each labelled with what the holder can do. Totals match the CKB Explorer cell by cell.
image2560×1972 318 KB
CKB still under the scripts of products that are gone or changed, reproducible with npm run snapshot.
2. Team Profile
Applicant: Ding, GitHub: ding99bt
Role: author and maintainer of Lifeboat.
Background: software engineer, 3+ years at Samsung R&D; researched the Stellar blockchain before moving to CKB.
Why me: Lifeboat is not an idea on paper. The scanner and the Nervos DAO exit already run, and every number in this proposal can be reproduced from the repository. I want to take it to the point where a holder of a dead product’s cells can get out on their own.
How I work: nothing is taken on trust.
Every scan is checked against the CKB Explorer (npm run compare).
Every transaction recipe runs end to end on a local devnet before testnet, with checks that fail when something is wrong.
Nothing signs on mainnet before review.
Project repository: GitHub - ding99bt/lifeboat · GitHub
Contact: Telegram @ding0x68
3. Project Background
When a CKB product shuts down, its users’ @ding0x68ells stay on chain. Some can be moved by the holder alone; some need the operator; for many, nobody has checked. Every time so far, the fix was a one-off, or nothing:
NexisDAO’s frontend shut down abruptly, and a community developer had to build dCKB Rescuer, an alternative frontend just for dCKB withdrawals (t/8369).
Godwoken and Force Bridge were sunset. After the exit window, Godwoken leftovers can no longer be withdrawn through its usual front end (t/8789).
USDI on CKB was discontinued (t/10417).
Portal Wallet’s site, ckb.pw, now redirects to an unrelated domain; its maintainers already had no capacity in 2023 (t/7008).
Live cells per script, from the CKB Explorer API (npm run snapshot, 17 Nov 2026):
image2272×632 76.2 KB
Spark’s Q3 report noted that few projects deal with what happens when centralized services stop responding or entry points are closed, and asked for practical work on it (t/11077). Lifeboat addresses exactly that disruption: the operator disappears (frontend, domain, wallet app or server) while the assets remain on chain.
Scenario. Someone deposited CKB into the Nervos DAO with Portal Wallet in 2021. Today they paste their old MetaMask address into Lifeboat. It shows the pw-lock cells and the deposit, explains that the deposit must be withdrawn first, builds each transaction, and MetaMask signs it. No team, server or custodian is needed.
4. Solution
Lifeboat runs entirely in the browser and talks to a CKB node directly (public nodes or the user’s own). It never holds keys or funds.
image2752×1344 395 KB
Scan: a CKB address, an old MetaMask address (its pw-lock and Omnilock addresses are derived, nothing is connected), or a wallet connected through CCC (JoyID, MetaMask, UniSat, OKX, UTXO Global…).
Label: every lock and type script gets a name and a status from CCC’s known scripts, the CKB Explorer’s script list and Lifeboat’s own dated notes (active / discontinued / not checked).
Report: CKB per group, what sits under a discontinued product, and what the holder can do.
Get out: an exit recipe builds the transaction and shows it in full: what it spends, what it creates, whether each output belongs to the user, and the fee. The user signs in their own wallet.
How it differs from what exists:
Neuron can close an empty sUDT account to recover its CKB, and offers a manual troubleshooting page for non-empty ones (t/7827): Neuron users only, sUDT only. Lifeboat is wallet-agnostic and covers xUDT.
The CCC demo app can sign almost anything, but it does not explain what each cell is or warn that a product is gone.
dCKB Rescuer solved one protocol once: 10 depositors took back 24 deposits (1.43M CKB) through it, and it stopped working in 2025 (https://talk.nervos.org/t/11016). Lifeboat is a registry of exits, plus a sheet that rates every protocol on whether a holder can leave alone.
secnev ( Spark Program | secnev — CKB-native risk observatory ) scores market and stablecoin risk. Tranfr ( Tranfr — Programmable Recovery for CKB ) and InheritVault ( InheritVault - A Simple Timelock Inheritance Vault on Nervos CKB (Web MVP) ) are recovery plans set up before anything goes wrong; Waymark ( Waymark — Recovering useful wallet state without starting from zero ) restores a wallet’s sync state. Lifeboat handles assets already stranded by a lost operator. These complement each other.
Explicitly out of scope: exits that need the operator (Godwoken leftovers, Force Bridge leftovers, USDI redemption); mainnet signing before review; an audit; an in-browser light client (stretch goal only).
5. Technical Approach
Stack: Vite, React, TypeScript, CCC (core library 1.23.1 and the CCC connector), Tailwind. Static build with relative paths, so it can be served from IPFS. Vitest for unit tests; a Node script for end-to-end runs.
Reading cells: findCellsByLock per lock, with data. A lock with more cells than the reading limit is cut short, but its Nervos DAO cells are always read in full. This was a real bug found on the way, now covered by a regression test.
Labels: CCC known scripts per network, the CKB Explorer list (keyed by type hash when there is one, because the same binary can be deployed twice: USDI is a deployment of the xUDT binary), and curated notes with dates and links.
Checks against the chain: npm run compare – scans with Lifeboat’s own code and compares every lock’s balance and cell count with the CKB Explorer. It matched on four real mainnet wallets, the largest with 183 cells.

image2272×632 76.2 KB

One question I expect, so I’ll answer it up front: apps built on CCC can already sign for pw-lock cells, so what does Lifeboat add?
They can, and Lifeboat uses the same CCC signer. Signing is not the missing piece. Knowing is. When a MetaMask account is connected, CCC includes its pw-lock address, so an app like app.ckbccc.com can spend those cells, and NervDAO handles Nervos DAO deposits for a connected wallet. But a holder only gets there if they already know that their old CKB is still on chain, that it sits under pw-lock (the lock behind Portal Wallet, whose site is gone), and that a Nervos DAO deposit under it has to be withdrawn before the CKB can move. Today nothing tells them that.
I checked how much this is about, using the public mainnet RPC (get_cells on the pw-lock code hash)
29,219 live pw-lock cells hold 281.8M CKB across 8,011 addresses.
6,700 of these addresses (84%), holding 141.6M CKB, have no live cell newer than 1 Jan 2024. 1,802 of them hold at least 1,000 CKB.
2,611 of the cells are Nervos DAO cells (172.5M CKB), which need the two-step withdrawal before they can move.
Idle does not mean lost. Some of these holders keep long-term DAO deposits and know exactly where their CKB is. For the others, the first step is to find out what is there, and that is what the live demo already does, read-only and without connecting anything: paste an Ethereum address at https://lifeboat-ckb.vercel.app and it derives the pw-lock address, lists what is there and names the product it belonged to.

Lifeboat is for a holder who is not sure what is left. It finds the assets, explains them and walks through a safe exit with a full preview. For a product that is gone, there is no original team left to build that exit, and Lifeboat reuses CCC for signing instead of competing with it.

recent_posts.author: psawyerberlin
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi Cecilia,
Thank you, I’m really glad you want to do this together.
You’re right, and it’s actually stronger than “three shares combined”. In CRT v0.2, release is public by design: at the deadline, each runner writes its private key into its Node Cell on-chain. From then on, anyone who has the descriptor can rebuild the payload. So the CRT payload should only ever mean “the deadline has passed”, never “this person is the heir”. Your two-input circuit is exactly right:
• heir secret → proves who is claiming
• CRT payload → proves the deadline passed (and that the owner didn’t cancel)
Neither one opens it alone, and the release channel no longer has to keep anything secret. That’s a much cleaner trust model.
This also fits well with revocation. If the owner cancels, the runners delete their keys and the payload can never be rebuilt, so the claim can never succeed, even if the heir secret has leaked. And before the deadline, a leaked heir secret is useless on its own.
One thing I’d like the issue to keep open: CRT should support both modes. Revocable is right for inheritance and dead-man-switch cases. Other uses, like voting, need the opposite: an irrevocable, threshold-only setup where nobody, not even the creator, can stop the release. Since the Alive Cell can use any lock, both modes work with the same scripts.
One small point for the design: I’d still bind the proof to the claim transaction (outputs/destination). That’s not to protect against the payload holders. It’s so that nobody can copy the heir’s proof from the mempool and send the claim to a different output.
For a fast end-to-end experiment, CRT has a testnet drill deployment where the grace period is 10 minutes instead of 24 hours, so a full create → release → claim cycle takes under an hour.

Feel free to add the circuit and verifying-key side whenever it suits you. I’ll be able to look at it properly in about two weeks, and then I’ll add the payload format and the drill deployment details.
Kind regards,
PSBerlin
